idiom_name: private (compile-time, erased) or # fields (hard private) plus the module export surface as the narrow door
implementation_notes: TypeScript's private and protected are checked only by the compiler: the handbook states that JavaScript runtime constructs like in or a simple property lookup still reach such a member, while ECMAScript private fields (#) 'remain private after compilation' and offer no bracket-notation escape, which it calls hard private. The attorney therefore has two layers: use private when the goal is build-time discipline about who may call what, accepting that any cast or plain-JS consumer walks around it, and # fields when the runtime must hold; then publish the narrow surface as the module's exports so the implementation class stays module-private. The hand-built attorney is still justified when one collaborator outside the module must be the only caller - TypeScript cannot express that - because no class other than the declaring one gets access to a private member, however the code is organised.
pitfalls: private and protected are erased: bracket access, an 'as any' cast or any plain-JavaScript consumer reads and writes the member at run time - only # members are hard private.

# members are per class and are not inherited: a subclass cannot touch the parent's # fields and no function outside the class body can name them, so the narrow surface has to be produced by a method of that class.

Keep module-private implementation types out of exported signatures: an exported attorney whose declaration emit names a non-exported type is not usable by consumers, and re-exports can widen the door further.
